summary: Mount Cartier fire lookout near Revelstoke, built about 1922 and little used for fire watch; standing in a 2014 article; reached by a 15 km trail or helicopter.

facts.status_note: Last described as standing in a 2014 Revelstoke Review article; Wikipedia says it still stands, undated.

access.note: The sources describe a hiking and biking trail and helicopter lifts to the summit; none mentions a closure or a permit.

visit.trail_note: 15 km trail from the lake to the lookout; the Revelstoke Review calls it the hardest Revelstoke-area lookout to reach.

events.note: Build year from Kevin Lavelle's research, as quoted by the Revelstoke Review; the trail and a telephone cable were probably put in a year earlier. The registry's builder claim (CP Rail) is not supported by these sources.
Believed to have gone unused after 1930 (Revelstoke Review). Wikipedia says it has not been used for fire detection since the 1930s.

evidence.quote: The peak is situated 13 km (8.1 mi) southeast of Revelstoke
Mount Cartier is a 2,610-metre (8,563-foot) mountain summit

evidence.supports: Lookout perched on a ledge on the south ridge
evidence.quote: The Mount Cartier fire lookout is perched on a ledge on the south ridge of the mountain

evidence.supports: Trail built in the early 1920s to reach a forestry lookout near the summit
evidence.quote: The trail up Mt. Cartier was built in the early-1920s to access a forestry lookout near the summit.

evidence.supports: Lavelle, a local forestry official, dates the lookout to 1922 and the trail a year earlier
evidence.quote: According to Kevin Lavelle, a local forestry official who has done a great deal of research on the history of lookouts, the Cartier lookout was built in 1922, though the trail, along with a telephone cable, was probably put in a year before.

evidence.supports: The 15 km trail is the hard way up; the helicopter is the easy way
evidence.quote: The hard way is up the 15-kilometre trail that snakes its way to the summit

evidence.supports: Trail and lookout constructed in the early 1920s (Wikipedia)
evidence.quote: The trail and lookout were constructed in the early 1920s

evidence.supports: Wikipedia says the lookout still stands (undated)
Registry says the tower was built by CP Rail
Lookout was not used for long; fires got established before detection
evidence.quote: Unfortunately, the Mt. Cartier forestry lookout was not utilized for long, as it soon became apparent that due to weather conditions, forest fires were able to get well established long before being detected from such a lofty vantage point,

evidence.supports: Not used for fire detection since the 1930s
evidence.quote: it hasn't been used for fire detection since the 1930s

evidence.supports: Believed unused after 1930; permanent lookout on Mount Sproat in 1956
evidence.quote: It is believed the Cartier lookout wasn't used after 1930, with a permanent lookout established on Mount Sproat to the south in 1956.

evidence.supports: Still standing; survived about 90 years and needed only a new roof
evidence.quote: The lookout remains, having withstood 90 years of winter and summer storms, with only the roof being replaced.

evidence.supports: Writer passed the lookout just before reaching the summit
evidence.quote: Just before reaching the summit of Cartier, we passed by the old lookout, still standing after all these years.

evidence.supports: Two ways up: helicopter, or the 15 km trail
evidence.quote: There are two ways to the top of Mount Cartier. The easy way is with a helicopter.

evidence.supports: Lookout is the hardest in the Revelstoke area to reach
evidence.quote: The Mount Cartier lookout is the hardest to access in the Revelstoke area.

evidence.supports: 15 km trail begins at the lake
evidence.quote: From the lake, a 15-kilometer trail leads to a fire lookout and the upper slopes.

evidence.supports: Helicopters lift mountain bikers to a helipad below the summit
evidence.quote: helicopters lifting mountain bikers to a helipad below the summit

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The registry says the tower was 'Built by CP Rail.' The Revelstoke Review describes a forestry lookout built in 1922 and does not name the railway. No source here names CP Rail as the builder. The story reports both accounts and does not adopt the registry claim.

sources.title: On lookout: The history of — and how to get to — Revelstoke's fire lookouts

notes_for_editor: The 1922 build year rests on Kevin Lavelle's research as quoted in a 2014 Revelstoke Review article; Wikipedia's early-1920s date agrees. The registry's 'Built by CP Rail' claim is not confirmed by the Review, which calls the lookout a forestry lookout and names no builder, so it is not adopted; a BC archives search could settle it. No source names the agency that managed the lookout, so no agency fact is set. The most recent condition report is from 2014; no source describes the site now. Tower height is not in these sources. The 'abandoned' event is a judgment for 'stopped being used for fire detection', based on the 'believed' wording in the Review. Grokipedia, a mirror of Wikipedia, was seen in search results but not used.
